title: Knowing what you know
hookLine: to know what you know and know what you don't: that is knowledge (Analects 2.17)
tomorrow: who should you copy, and what do you do with a bad example?

lines: HALF OF IT IS NOT KNOWING.
cards: In a meeting someone drops an acronym, and the whole table nods. Nobody wants to be the one who asks what it stands for. The Analects has a puzzle about exactly that.

Confucius turns to one student, Zilu, whose personal name is Yu, and offers to teach him what knowledge is. Then he gives a definition that's half about not knowing. Why would knowledge need not-knowing inside it?
And why say it to Zilu, of all people?

teach.h: HOLD WHAT YOU KNOW. ALLOW WHAT YOU DON'T.
teach.b: Here's the line, in James Legge's translation: "When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge." Now meet Zilu in another passage.
Confucius says that if he governed, his first task would be to set names right, so that words match things.
Zilu shoots back: you're wide of the mark! Confucius answers him bluntly: how unpolished you are, Yu. A gentleman holds back about what he doesn't know.
So the puzzle solves itself, on one reading: the definition was cut to fit the student. Elsewhere Confucius says Zilu loves daring even more than he does.
Brave, quick people fill gaps with confidence, and it often works, until it doesn't. Confucius doesn't tell him to know more.

teach.h: THE JUNZI KNOWS WHERE HIS KNOWING STOPS.
teach.b: He tells him to see where his knowing stops.
The teaching, plainly: in the Confucian tradition, the junzi, the exemplary person, is honest about the edge of their knowledge, because when words don't match things, actions go wrong too.
One for tonight: Confucius's definition of knowledge has two halves, and the second half is saying I don't know.
In the Analects that sentence isn't a hole in your knowledge. It's part of it.

how: Readers of the Analects take 2.17 as a check on honesty in learning; in the Confucian tradition, admitting the limits of what you know belongs to the exemplary person, the junzi.

games.q: what does “knowing what you know” mean?
o: doubting everything until it's fully proven
holding what you know and admitting what you don't
knowing enough to answer any question asked

games.q: Zilu and the definition: tap the pairs.
p: the quick, bold student, called Yu
allow that you don't know it
holds back about what he doesn't know

s: Confucius tells Zilu that knowledge means knowing more
he says knowledge includes allowing what you don't know.
Zilu once told Confucius he was wide of the mark
in 13.3, and Confucius answers that a gentleman holds back about what he doesn't know.
Confucius wanted names set right, so words match things
in 13.3 he says it would be his first task if he governed.

games.q: a new coworker asks how a system works that you only half understand. what's the Analects answer?
o: explain the half you know, and say plainly where your knowing stops.
explain all of it confidently; doubt makes you look unready.
say you know nothing about it, so you can't be wrong.
games.why: 2.17: hold what you know, allow what you don't. the two halves together are knowledge; hiding the half you know isn't it either.

practice: Think of one thing you've been nodding along to: a word, a fact, something at work or at home. For these two minutes, say it quietly to yourself: I don't know this yet.
Then picture the one person you could ask, and the exact question.

wordCard.voice: Knowing what you know: Confucius's knowledge in two halves, the part you hold and the edge you admit.

orig.note: Chinese zhi, to know, knowledge: the word Confucius repeats through Analects 2.17.

carryVoice: Keep this one: that is knowledge, and knowing where your knowing stops counts too. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge.

sources.ref: Analects 5.6 (Zilu is fonder of daring than Confucius)
